id: To J.G. On the News of His Marriage

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My Love? alas! I must not call you Mine, But to your envy’d Bride that Name resign: I must forget your lovely melting Charms, And be for ever Banisht from your Arms: For ever? oh! the Horror of that Sound! It gives my bleeding Heart a deadly wound: While I might hope, although my Hope was vain, It gave some Ease to my unpitty’d Pain, But now your Hymen doth all Hope exclude, And but to think is Sin; yet you intrude On every Thought; if I but close my Eyes, Methinks your pleasing Form besides me lies; With every Sigh I gently breath your Name, Yet no ill Thoughts pollute my hallow’d Flame; ’Tis pure and harmless, as a Lambent Fire, And never mingled with a warm Desire: All I have now to ask of Bounteous Heaven, Is, that your Perjuries may be forgiven: That she who you have with your Nuptials blest, As She’s the Happiest Wife, may prove the Best: That all our Joys may light on you alone, Then I can be contented to have none: And never wish that you shou’d kinder be, Than now and then, to cast a Thought on Me: And, Madam, though the Conquest you have won, Over my Strephon, has my hopes undone; I’le daily beg of Heaven, he may be Kinder to You, than he has been to Me.

outputs.L2: Beloved—though sadly I can no longer claim you as My own, and must hand that title over to the bride who now takes my place. I am forced to push aside the memory of your beautiful, tender attractions, and be cast out from your embrace permanently. Permanently? Oh, how dreadful those words are! They strike my grieving heart like a fatal blow. When I still had something to hope for—even though such hope was pointless—it brought a little comfort to my sorrow that no one takes pity on. But now that you are wed, every possibility of hope is shut off, and merely dwelling on you has become sinful. Even so, you invade all my thinking; whenever I shut my eyes, I imagine your delightful shape resting beside me. Each breath I take softly whispers your name, yet no wicked notions taint my sacred devotion. It burns clean and innocent, like a gentle flickering flame, never tainted by heated longing. The only request I now make of generous Heaven is that your broken vows might be pardoned—and that the woman you've honored with marriage, being the most fortunate of wives, may also turn out to be the finest. Let every happiness fall upon you alone, and I will be satisfied to receive none myself. I'll never ask you to show me more tenderness than to occasionally spare a thought for me. And, Madam, although your victory in winning my Strephon has destroyed all my hopes, I will pray to Heaven every day that he treats you with more kindness than he ever showed to me.
outputs.L3:
# A Lament of Renounced Love

With a heavy heart, the speaker mourns that she must relinquish her beloved, surrendering him to the bride whose fortune she cannot help but envy. She acknowledges that she must forever renounce any claim she once believed she held upon him, letting go of the man she loves and accepting that he now belongs to another.

It is the permanence of this separation that causes her the deepest anguish. The finality of his marriage wounds her profoundly, for it extinguishes every last ember of hope to which she had so desperately clung. What torments her is not merely the parting itself, but the knowledge that it can never be undone—that the door has closed upon her forever.

Though she strives to banish him from her mind, she finds it impossible to forget him. His memory intrudes upon her without mercy, forcing itself into her every waking moment. When she closes her eyes, his image appears beside her; in every sigh that escapes her lips, she feels his presence lingering still. He haunts her thoughts as persistently as breath itself.

Yet she is careful to insist upon the purity of her affection. Her love, she maintains, is entirely innocent and harmless, untouched by any lustful or improper desire. It burns not as a consuming fire, but as a gentle, tender flame—chaste in its nature and honorable in its intent.

In a final act of selflessness, she sets aside her own grief to offer her blessings. She prays for his forgiveness, and she wishes genuine happiness upon his wife. Asking nothing for herself, she hopes only that he might, from time to time, spare her a passing thought. And with quiet dignity, she expresses her deepest wish: that he might treat his new bride with greater kindness and tenderness than he ever showed to her.
outputs.L4:
# The Lament for Strephon: An Exploration of Selfless Love and Resignation

## The Speaker's Heartbreak

At the heart of this poem lies a woman whose world has been irrevocably altered by loss. Her beloved, named Strephon—a name that carries with it the pastoral, idealized associations of romantic poetry—has chosen another woman to be his wife. This union, sealed through the binding permanence of marriage, represents not merely a temporary separation but a final and unyielding conclusion to whatever hopes the speaker once nurtured. Her grief is raw and immediate, coloring every line with the ache of a heart that has been wounded beyond ordinary consolation.

## The Power of Direct Address

Rather than mourning in abstraction, the speaker turns to direct address, speaking as though her beloved and perhaps her rival stand before her. This intimate mode of communication lends the poem an urgency and emotional immediacy that draws the reader into the very center of her suffering. Through these emotional appeals, she lays bare the anguish of her situation, refusing to hide behind pretense or pride. Her words become a vessel for both her pain and her dignity, as she navigates the delicate line between confessing her sorrow and maintaining her composure.

## Renunciation Without Diminishment

One of the most striking qualities of the speaker's lament is her willingness to renounce any claim upon Strephon. She acknowledges that he now belongs to another, and she does not contest this reality or attempt to reclaim what has been lost. Yet in surrendering her claim, she simultaneously insists upon the essential purity of her love. Hers is not a possessive or jealous devotion that demands reciprocity; rather, it is a love unselfish in its very nature. She loves not for what she might receive in return, but for the sake of the beloved himself. This distinction elevates her emotional experience, transforming her heartbreak into something noble rather than merely pitiable.

## The Act of Self-Sacrifice

The poem reaches its emotional climax in the speaker's ultimate resolution. Rather than harboring bitterness toward the woman who has taken her place, she resolves to pray for her rival's happiness. This gesture represents a profound act of self-sacrifice, for it requires the speaker to set aside her own desires and wounded feelings in favor of goodwill toward the very person who has, however innocently, become the instrument of her sorrow. Alongside this prayer for her rival, she also seeks forgiveness for her lost lover—an acknowledgment that reflects both humility and an enduring tenderness toward the man she cannot cease to love.

## Emotional Resignation and Devotion

In these final movements, the poem underscores the extraordinary depth of the speaker's unrequited devotion. Her resignation is not the resignation of despair or defeat, but rather a quiet, dignified acceptance of a love that must remain forever unfulfilled. By choosing prayer over resentment and blessing over bitterness, she demonstrates that true love, in its highest form, seeks the happiness of the beloved even at the cost of one's own. The poignancy of this conclusion lies precisely in this selflessness: the speaker gains nothing for herself, yet she offers everything of her heart. In doing so, she transforms her personal tragedy into a testament of pure and enduring devotion.
outputs.L5:
# Love, Mine, But

Love arrived quietly, the way morning light slips through a window before you're fully awake. I didn't ask for it, didn't plan for it, but there it was—warming everything it touched.

*Mine.* That's the word my heart whispered when I first understood what had happened. Not in a possessive way, not in a way that sought to cage or control, but in the tender sense that something precious had chosen to stay. This feeling was mine to hold, mine to nurture, mine to protect.

But love is rarely simple.

But it asks things of us we didn't know we could give. But it stretches our patience, tests our understanding, and holds a mirror to our deepest fears. Love is beautiful, yes—but it is also brave. It requires us to stay when leaving would be easier, to forgive when holding grudges feels justified, to grow when comfort begs us to remain the same.

I called it mine, but I've come to learn that love isn't truly a possession. It's a partnership, a dance between two people who choose each other again and again. What's mine is only mine because it's freely given, and it remains only if I give freely in return.

So I hold this love gently now. Mine, but not owned. Cherished, but not clutched. Because the truest love isn't about what we can keep—it's about what we're willing to share.

And that, perhaps, is the most beautiful paradox of all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Restoration-era poem in heroic couplets in which a woman laments losing her lover Strephon to another woman he has married.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Forsaken Nymph; or, Strephon Wed**

Ye gentle shades, that heard my Strephon swear
By all the powers that rule the yielding fair,
Bear witness now how false those vows are grown,
And mourn a faith more fickle than my own.
That tongue which once could every doubt remove
Has spent on her the coin it stamped for love;
Those eyes, whose light was constant as the sun,
Now shine for two, where once they burned for one.

How oft beneath yon melancholy tree
He carved a heart, and wrote it—*Thine and Me*!
The bark has healed, the letters worn away,
As all his passion perished in a day.
The very brook that murmured to our vow
Runs cold, and mocks my lonely sorrow now;
Each flower he plucked to grace my careless hair
Lies dead, and I lie deader in despair.

And who is she that wears my rifled bliss?
No brighter cheek, no softer lip than this;
No warmer breast to shelter his unrest,
Yet hers the ring, and hers the bridal guest.
Perhaps her portion swelled the parson's zeal—
For gold can gild what beauty ne'er could steal;
So Strephon, wiser than his heart could be,
Sold to her dower the love he owed to me.

Go, happy bride, and count thy purchase o'er,
Nor grudge the sighs he sighed at my poor door;
Enjoy the man—but know, when passion's past,
The vows he broke for thee will break as fast.
That heart which changed to win thee, changed once more,
Shall change again, and leave thee, as before.

For me, no altar and no torch shall shine;
The willow, not the myrtle, shall be mine.
I'll seek some grot where cheerful day ne'er came,
And teach the echoes but one faithless name;
There, till kind death shall close these weeping eyes,
Lament the swain, and curse him as he dies—
Yet, even in cursing, feel the treacherous smart,
And love the wretch that broke a truer heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a 17th-century love complaint where the speaker renounces her beloved to his new bride and wishes them happiness despite her broken heart.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Complaint, and Farewell to My False Love**

Go, take her hand, and let the sacred vow
Bind up that heart which once was pledged to me;
I will not curse, nor cloud thy nuptial brow,
Though all my summer withers in the tree.

She wears the ring I dreamed should grace my own,
She keeps the smiles I hoarded in my breast;
Yet shall I stand, forsaken and alone,
And bless the arms wherein thou art possessed.

I do not envy her that gentle face,
Nor grudge the fortune that hath made her thine;
May Heaven pour on her its every grace,
And give her all the joys that were not mine.

Let no cold shadow of my grief come near
To dim the tapers of your bridal night;
I'll shed in secret each remembering tear,
That you may laugh unwounded in the light.

Only, when years have silvered o'er thy head,
And she sits crowned beside thy quiet fire,
Think once—but once—upon the love long dead
That asked no dower but thy whole desire.

Farewell. I loose thee, as the wounded dove
Looses the arrow buried in her side;
Go, be thou happy in another's love—
I could not live thy scorn, and so I died.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Aphra Behn about unrequited love and the pain of watching one's love marry someone else.
counterfactuals.output:
**Upon Seeing My Love Wed Another**

Now must I stand where once I hoped to kneel,
And watch another take the vows I sought;
The wound is deep, yet deeper still I feel
The cruel sweetness of forbidden thought.

Ah, Damon! When thy hand she gently took,
Mine trembled with a passion none could see;
Thou gav'st to her that soft, consenting look
Which all my soul had begged to fall on me.

The garlands bloom, the merry bells resound,
And every heart but mine is bid rejoice;
I smile the smile that hides a mortal wound,
And still my sighs, and still my breaking voice.

Let Hymen's torch burn bright above thy head—
For me it lights a slow, consuming fire;
Each vow ye speak, some hope of mine lies dead,
And on that altar burns my whole desire.

Yet think not, Damon, that I curse thy joy,
Or wish thy Bride one moment's want of grace;
I would not this fair happiness destroy,
Though I be banished from thy heart's embrace.

But when the feast is done, and midnight steals
Its silence o'er thy chamber, warm and blest,
Remember not the sorrow Silvia feels,
Nor how she loved thee more than all the rest.

I'll to some shade where none may mark my tears,
And there resign the treasure I have lost;
Love gave me nothing in my hopeful years
But this: to know at last how dear the cost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a mournful verse epistle addressed to a former lover and his new wife, using archaic spelling and language from the late 1600s.
counterfactuals.output:
**An Epistle, Writ in Sorrowe to My Former Loue, and to Her He Hath Now Wed**

*Anno 1687*

To thee, deare Faithlesse, and thy new-made Bride,
I send these lines, though Griefe would haue them hide;
For what auailes it that my Penne complaine,
When thou art gon, and I but weepe in vaine?

Yet suffer, Sir, one mournfull word to fall
From her that lou'd thee once, and lost thee all.
Thou swor'st (dost thou remember?) by the Skie,
That sooner should the Starres forget to flie,
The Sunne grow cold, the Sea forsake his Shore,
Then thou prooue false—and now thou lou'st no more.

O happie Wife, that weares what once was mine!
Take thou his Hand, his Name, his House, his Vine;
Take thou the Vowes that were to me first sworne,
And weare my Ring, though it were mine ere morne.
I grudge thee not; onely, I pray thee, know
Thou treadst a Path where I did weeping goe.

When at the Altar thou didst plight thy Troth,
Methought I heard the Ecchoe of his Oath—
That selfe-same Oath he breath'd to me of yore
Beneath the Elme, vpon the Riuers shore.
The Elme yet standes; the Riuer runneth still;
Onely his Heart hath chang'd, and broke my Will.

Bee happie, then, and may no Winters cold
Come neare thy Ioyes till thou art gray and old.
But if, some Euen, when the Candle's low,
Thou see him sit and sigh, and know not whoe—
Aske him not why; for I shall then bee Dust,
And he doth thinke on Vowes, and broken Trust.

Farewell, false Loue; farewell, thou fortunate Faire;
I leaue to thee the Ioye, to me the Care.
Liue thou belou'd; and when thou com'st to dye,
Bee mourn'd of Him—as I now mourne, and sigh.

*Thy sometime Loue, now Nothing,*
*E. M.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about a pure, chaste love that must be given up, ending with the speaker praying that her faithless lover treats his wife better than he treated her.
counterfactuals.output:
**When You Are Wed**

I loved you with a love unstained by touch,
A quiet fire that never sought its due;
I gave you all my faith, and asked not much—
Only the small, sweet certainty of you.

We walked through summers innocent and bright,
Our hands unclasped, our hearts a single flame;
I kept my heart as chaste as morning light,
And thought that you would keep for me the same.

But faith, I've learned, is not a thing you own—
You spent mine freely, then you turned away,
And left me with my honor and alone
To gather up the ruins of the day.

So go. I will not curse you as you leave,
Nor let my sorrow settle into hate;
I have no bitter portion to bequeath,
Only a prayer I offer to your fate:

That she who wears the ring I never wore
May find in you a truer, gentler man;
That you will guard her heart, and something more—
Will love her better than you loved me. Then

When you have made her happy all your years,
And she has never wept the tears I've wept,
Perhaps you'll pause, and think of me, and hear
The promise to another soul you kept—

And know one woman loved you, clean and whole,
Who asked for nothing but a faithful friend,
And gave you, freely, all her quiet soul,
And blessed you, even at the bitter end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
